I ran one random-circuit sampling job on IQM's free Garnet test device, garnet:mock. The job ID is 01a16040-47ed-7334-94bc-296beff98394. It used 1000 shots and cost 0 credits.

What I ran: I used 8 connected Garnet qubits, QB1, QB2, QB3, QB4, QB5, QB8, QB9 and QB10. The circuit has 12 layers of two-qubit CZ gates, 30 CZ gates in total. Before each layer, every qubit gets a random half-turn rotation about one of three axes. That gives 104 single-qubit gates. I wrote the circuit in IQM's native gates so that it runs on exactly these qubits. I then worked out the exact chance of each of the 256 possible 8-bit outcomes on a laptop.

The scores: xeb_ideal is 1.058. That is the score a perfect quantum computer would get on this circuit. xeb_measured is -0.426. That is the score of the 1000 samples the mock device returned.

What the score means: linear XEB checks whether the device's outputs land on the outcomes that the circuit makes more likely than average. A score near 0 means the samples look like random guessing. A score near 1 means the samples follow the circuit's ideal pattern. Real hardware lands in between, and the score drops roughly as the chance that no gate error happened. Google's 2019 experiment on 53 qubits scored about 0.002. That small score was still clearly above 0.

Why this result is low: the mock device does not simulate the circuit. It returns made-up bitstrings. Here it returned only 8 different patterns, and those happen to be less likely than average under the ideal distribution. So the score is below 0. That is expected for a test device, and it shows the score works. Samples that do not come from the circuit do not get credit. To see a positive score, the same circuit would need to run on the real garnet QPU, which costs credits. I did not do that because you asked for the free test device.

Why 8 qubits is easy and 50 is not: a laptop simulates 8 qubits by tracking 2^8 = 256 complex numbers. That takes well under a second. Each added qubit doubles the count. At 50 qubits there are about 10^15 numbers, which needs petabytes of memory. At 53 or more qubits, the best supercomputer methods take a very long time or need clever shortcuts. A quantum computer does not store those numbers. It just runs the gates and produces samples. This gap is the reason random circuit sampling is the task where quantum computers have been shown to beat classical supercomputers.
